Peri-Fuse

A lightweight, self-contained LLM observability server — the open-source platform for tracing, evaluating, and debugging AI applications.

Peri-Fuse uses embedded Turso + Drizzle by default, with no external infrastructure (no ClickHouse, Redis, S3, or BullMQ). You can optionally replace local databases with remote Turso using a URL and auth token. It's designed for local development, small teams, and edge deployments.

This release initializes fresh .turso.db databases; existing SQLite files are not automatically converted or deleted. To preserve legacy data, stop the service and run bash scripts/migrate-legacy-db.sh --offline. See legacy migration for safe inspection, large-database handling and resuming, and embedded Turso storage for pinned versions and migrations. Requires Bun 1.4.2 or newer to run the server, the gateway, and the service CLI. The build and test toolchain (pnpm, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest) still runs on Node.js 22.12.0 or newer — see runtime requirements.

Features

  • LLM observability (traces, spans, generations, scores)
  • OpenTelemetry (OTLP) ingestion
  • Public REST API compatible with Langfuse SDKs
  • Lightweight web dashboard (Vite + React)
  • Self-contained deployment through Docker or the repository-local service CLI
  • MCP resources and HTTP integration through the built-in /mcp endpoint

Quick Start

Choose the workflow that matches how you want to run Peri-Fuse.

Docker

The included Compose configuration runs the published image and persists all data in ./data:

docker compose up -d

# Verify the API, follow logs, or stop the service
curl http://localhost:23332/api/public/health
docker compose logs -f
docker compose down

Open the dashboard at http://localhost:23332. Port 23332 is used when LITE_SERVER_PORT is absent from both the host environment and .env. Setting that variable changes the container listener and published port together. docker compose down leaves the bind-mounted ./data directory intact.

The production Docker image runs the server and its health check with Bun 1.4.2 on Debian, and keeps Node.js 22 in the image for the one-off legacy SQLite migration (scripts/migrate-legacy-db.sh, which mixes node:sqlite with the Turso driver). Dependency installation and compilation use Node.js/pnpm build stages; the runtime image only receives production dependencies and built assets. The release workflow builds both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 (Apple Silicon).

The dashboard defaults to light mode and automatically activates Default Project on a fresh visit. Saved theme and valid project selections are preserved; stale project selections are replaced before data pages load.

Source development

Source development requires Bun 1.4.2 or newer to run the API server, Node.js 22.12.0 or newer for the build/test toolchain, and pnpm 10:

pnpm install
pnpm dev

The API runs at http://localhost:23432, and the Vite dashboard runs at http://localhost:5173 with /api proxied to the API server. SQLite schemas and the initial workspace are created automatically when the server starts.

To manage a production build from this checkout as a background service:

pnpm install
pnpm build
pnpm svc:start
pnpm svc:status
pnpm svc:logs
pnpm svc:stop

These commands use the CLI built from this repository; they do not require a global npm installation. They launch the CLI with Bun, so the managed background server also runs on Bun. The service defaults to http://localhost:23332, but the CLI loads .env and honors LITE_SERVER_PORT when it is set.

Project Structure

peri-fuse/
├── packages/
│   ├── shared/       # SQLite domain logic, ingestion, queries, and OTLP
│   ├── server/       # Hono HTTP server and production web host
│   ├── gateway/      # Project-scoped LLM proxy gateway
│   ├── web/          # Vite + React dashboard
│   └── cli/          # Background service manager
├── Dockerfile        # Multi-stage production image
├── docker-compose.yml
├── LICENSE            # MIT
└── NOTICE             # Attribution to Langfuse GmbH

Environment Variables

See .env.example for a ready-to-copy set of common options. Key variables:

Variable Default Description
LITE_SERVER_PORT 23332 API and dashboard port. The root pnpm dev script explicitly uses 23432.
PERIFUSE_HOME ~/.peri-fuse Persistent data directory. The Docker image uses /app/data, bound to ./data by Compose.
DATABASE_URL file:<PERIFUSE_HOME>/langfuse.turso.db Auth and metadata SQLite database.
TURSO_DATABASE_URL unset Optional remote Turso URL for all three database domains.
TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN unset Required auth token when a remote URL is configured.
LANGFUSE_SQLITE_DB_PATH <PERIFUSE_HOME>/telemetry.turso.db Trace, observation, and score SQLite database.
SALT generated and persisted API-key hash salt stored at <PERIFUSE_HOME>/.salt when unset.
LITE_LARGE_RESPONSE_THRESHOLD_BYTES 1048576 Response-size warning threshold in bytes.
PERIFUSE_TELEMETRY_RETENTION_DAYS disabled Optional retention period; unset or 0 disables automatic purging.

To use remote Turso, add these settings to .env (or export them before starting the service):

TURSO_DATABASE_URL=libsql://your-database-your-org.turso.io
TURSO_AUTH_TOKEN=your-database-token

Metadata, telemetry, and Gateway then share that remote database, including search workers. For separate databases or mixed local/remote storage, use TURSO_METADATA_DATABASE_URL,TURSO_TELEMETRY_DATABASE_URL, or TURSO_GATEWAY_DATABASE_URL, with the corresponding TURSO_<ROLE>_AUTH_TOKEN if needed. Role settings override global settings, which override legacy local paths. Startup applies migrations to a fresh database; existing local data is not uploaded. Connection/auth failures never silently fall back to local storage. Keep SALT and GATEWAY_ENCRYPTION_KEY stable across hosts, or preserve PERIFUSE_HOME. See storage configuration for details.

The checked-in .env.example explicitly selects port 23432 for source development. Copying it unchanged also overrides the CLI and Compose defaults, so adjust or comment out LITE_SERVER_PORT when you want the production default.

MCP

Peri-Fuse exposes the Langfuse skill as MCP resources from the same server as the dashboard and API. Start the production service with pnpm svc:start and configure an MCP client with http://localhost:23332/mcp; source development uses http://localhost:23432/mcp. The MCP endpoint is a public read-only skill resource endpoint and requires no credentials. Data API requests continue to use a project-scoped API key. The checked-in .mcp.json contains both local endpoints without authentication headers. See packages/langfuse-mcp/README.md for the optional Node stdio adapter.

The server serves a real file from the built web assets when the requested static path exists. For known web pages, an explicit Accept: text/html GET or HEAD request receives the SPA index.html. Unknown page/API paths, missing assets, and /.well-known/* discovery paths receive a JSON 404 response; existing API authentication still returns its normal JSON errors. The MCP endpoint supports both MCP 2026-07-28 and stateless 2025-11-25 clients. It only distributes skill resources; analysis scripts are instructions for the MCP client to run and are never executed by the server. OAuth discovery is not provided.

Performance

Peri-Fuse is optimized to handle production-scale workloads on a single SQLite file. Benchmarked at 250K traces / 1.13M observations / 1.6 GB:

Endpoint Latency Notes
Traces list 6 ms Indexed pagination
Observations list 24 ms Covering index scan
Sessions list 44 ms Two-phase query
Users list 85 ms Materialized aggregates
Dashboard 219 ms 30-day bounded analytics
Trace detail 1 ms PK lookup
Session detail 26 ms Batched observation fetch

Provenance: the table above was recorded at commit 66bc32b (2026-07-30) without a documented host, corpus, or measurement method, and the 1.6 GB dataset behind it is not checked in. Treat the numbers as historical orientation, not as a reproducible result: they cannot be re-measured from this repository, and the session list has since been rewritten. The harness-backed numbers below are the ones to keep current.

packages/server/src/__tests__/sessions-query-plan.test.ts validates the session list against a frozen pre-rewrite baseline on a 1,000-trace corpus (row-for-row equivalence plus query plans and cache-miss latency). packages/server/src/__tests__/sessions-scale-bench.test.ts reuses the same route capture on 100K/1M traces, and sessions-scale-diagnostic.test.ts measures the raw statement cost beyond the read pool's 30s budget. The optional standard-SQLite engine (PERIFUSE_ENGINE=sqlite) only runs under Bun, outside the Node vitest suite, so sessions-scale-bun-driver.ts repeats the same corpus/route/percentile measurement there (engine contrast below). The scale harnesses are opt-in, so the default test run stays fast:

cd packages/server
npx vitest run src/__tests__/sessions-query-plan.test.ts                          # 1K equivalence + plan + latency
PERIFUSE_BENCH_TRACES=100000 npx vitest run src/__tests__/sessions-scale-bench.test.ts
PERIFUSE_BENCH_TRACES=1000000 npx vitest run src/__tests__/sessions-scale-bench.test.ts
# deep measurement (bypasses the 30s read-pool budget; prints full SQL, plans, raw statement ms):
PERIFUSE_READ_WORKERS=0 PERIFUSE_BENCH_TRACES=1000000 npx vitest run src/__tests__/sessions-scale-diagnostic.test.ts

The harnesses seed a dedicated project through the public ingestion API (1K) or a direct bulk loader (100K/1M), run ANALYZE, and the benchmark samples 50 cache-miss requests of the default 50-row page plus the underlying list/count statements. Measured 2026-10-11 on macOS, Apple silicon (18 cores, 48 GiB RAM), Node 26.9.0, default embedded Turso engine, throwaway .test database,X-Cache: MISS, n=50 after 5 warmups (review §12 targets: request p95 ≤ 100 ms, p99 ≤ 250 ms). Request figures are percentiles over the measured samples; statement figures are p50, except the 1M entries, which are single deep-diagnostic measurements:

Corpus Scenario Request p50 Request p95 Request p99 list stmt count stmt §12 budget
1K traces / 200 sessions default order 3.39 ms 23.23 ms 44.42 ms 2.69 ms — met
1K traces / 200 sessions orderBy=totalCost.desc 3.76 ms 9.52 ms 23.23 ms 2.59 ms — met
100K traces / 20K sessions default order 46.03 ms 57.91 ms 78.14 ms 29.92 ms 14.06 ms met
100K traces / 20K sessions orderBy=totalCost.desc 134.75 ms 152.74 ms 155.51 ms 115.15 ms 15.46 ms request p95 missed
1M traces / 200K sessions default order route 503 — — 214,020 ms 1,469 ms list statement exceeds the 30s read-pool budget
1M traces / 200K sessions orderBy=totalCost.desc route 503 — — >300 s, interrupted — list statement does not finish

Notes:

  • The metric-ranked sort aggregates every session's metrics before it can rank a page, so at 100K it already exceeds the p95 budget. That is the design tradeoff recorded in review §3.3; the planned session_summary projection is the follow-up if the budget must hold. The miss is not a single-run artifact: three runs landed p95 = 152.7, 175.1, and 188.7 ms (the table quotes the fastest run).
  • At 1M traces the Turso planner flips the trace_metrics join from the (project_id, trace_id) primary-key index to idx_trace_metrics_ts (project_id=?), so every outer row scans the project's whole metrics prefix (~900K entries): the default page statement needs ~214 s for 50 rows — 30 ms at 100K — and the route answers 503 once the read pool's 30 s statement budget expires. System SQLite 3.51.0 (CLI) plans the same SQL on the same database file with the primary-key index and executes it in ~3.8 s, so the flip costs roughly 56x here; fixing it removes the planner penalty but not the seconds-scale 1M aggregation, so the §12 budget still needs the materialized session projection. The flip reproduces across runs (both scenarios, sqlite_stat1 populated), and system SQLite picks the primary-key index for both scenario queries.
  • The 1K frozen-baseline (pre-rewrite) statement measures p50 ≈ 182–186 ms at 1K traces versus 2.6–2.7 ms for the current page statement.

Swapping embedded Turso for Bun's built-in bun:sqlite removes the 1M planner problem but not the aggregation cost. Same corpora and host, Bun 1.4.2, default read pool, same capture and percentile logic through the Bun driver:

cd packages/server
PERIFUSE_ENGINE=sqlite PERIFUSE_BENCH_TRACES=100000 bun --bun src/__tests__/sessions-scale-bun-driver.ts
PERIFUSE_ENGINE=sqlite PERIFUSE_BENCH_TRACES=1000000 bun --bun src/__tests__/sessions-scale-bun-driver.ts
Corpus Scenario Request p50 Request p95 Request p99 list stmt p50 count stmt p50 §12 budget
100K traces / 20K sessions default order 30.50 ms 33.61 ms 35.28 ms 20.82 ms 8.96 ms met
100K traces / 20K sessions orderBy=totalCost.desc 81.99 ms 96.25 ms 100.24 ms 77.10 ms 9.66 ms request p95 on the line
1M traces / 200K sessions default order 263.07 ms 272.01 ms 275.56 ms 176.62 ms 84.32 ms request p95 missed
1M traces / 200K sessions orderBy=totalCost.desc 795.25 ms 814.59 ms 905.25 ms 710.17 ms 84.85 ms request p95 missed

Notes:

  • The Turso planner flip does not occur: with sqlite_stat1 populated, both 1M scenarios keep SEARCH tm USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_trace_metrics_1 (project_id=? AND trace_id=?), both routes answer 200 instead of 503, and the default-order list statement drops from 214,020 ms (Turso) to 176.62 ms (~1,200x). The flip disappears; the seconds-scale 1M aggregation does not.
  • 100K default order met the budget in all three runs (p95 = 30.59, 33.61, 36.88 ms; the table quotes the middle run). The metric-ranked sort sat on the line: p95 = 83.32 (pass), 96.25 (pass), 109.40 (miss) ms versus 152.74–188.70 ms on Turso — the swap removes most of the flip-driven cost at 100K too, but the §3.3 design gap remains.
  • The 1M rows quote the clean rerun; the first run, with leftover benchmark processes on the host, measured default p95 760.76 / p99 2,270.04 ms and metric p95 1,077.30 ms, i.e. the budget miss is robust to host noise while the margin is not. §12 at 1M still needs the materialized session_summary projection.

Optimization techniques

  • Materialized trace_metrics table — per-trace cost/token aggregates maintained incrementally on ingestion, eliminating full-table GROUP BY over millions of observation rows.
  • Two-phase pagination — list endpoints first resolve the page of IDs using lightweight trace-level indexes, then JOIN metrics only for the selected page (avoids aggregating the entire dataset).
  • Batched observation fetch — session detail loads all trace observations in a single IN (...) query instead of N+1 per-trace calls.
  • Time-bounded analytics — dashboard model/level breakdowns are scoped to the last 30 days, preventing unbounded full-table scans.
  • Covering indexes — purpose-built composite indexes (start_time + total_cost, type + start_time + model, etc.) allow index-only scans for aggregation queries.
  • ANALYZE -aware planner — indexes are designed to avoid SQLite query-planner regressions from conflicting candidate indexes.

License

MIT — see LICENSE. Based on Langfuse by Langfuse GmbH.
